procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated with a petition filed directly in the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The initial petition challenged the detention order dated August 29, 1968, made under section 3(1)(a)(ii) of the Preventive Detention Act.  Later, the petition was amended to also challenge a fresh detention order dated August 28, 1969, issued under the same section of the Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text. The case went directly to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initially granted time to the State of Assam to provide full material related to the first detention order. However, before the next hearing, a new detention order was issued. The petitioner then amended his petition to challenge the new order as well. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the petition and ordered the petitioner to be set at liberty, finding the detention order dated August 28, 1969, to be invalid under section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act.

directions: The petitioner shall be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether a fresh detention order under Section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act is valid if it is not based on fresh facts that have arisen after the date of expiry of the previous detention.

facts: A petitioner was under a detention order that was set to expire on August 29, 1969.
On August 28, 1969, one day before the previous order expired, the State issued a fresh detention order against the same person.
The State did not claim that this new order was based on any facts that had arisen *after* the expiry of the previous order.
The State did allege that the petitioner maintained links with associates while in custody, but these were facts that arose *during* the period of detention, not after its expiry.
law: Section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, permits a fresh detention order to be made against a person after a previous order has expired or been revoked.
However, this is only allowed in cases where "fresh facts have arisen after the date of revocation or expiry" on which the new order is based.
The court interprets this to mean that facts that arise *during* the period of a previous detention are not relevant for justifying a new order under Section 13(2).
application: The court applied the strict requirement of Section 13(2) to the facts of the case.
It noted that the fresh order was passed on August 28, 1969, a day *before* the previous order expired.
The court reasoned that it was logically impossible for this new order to be based on facts that had arisen *after* the expiry date, as the expiry had not yet occurred.

The court also dismissed the allegation that the petitioner maintained links while in custody as a valid ground, because this was a fact that arose *during* the detention period, not *after* its expiry, and therefore did not satisfy the requirements of Section 13(2).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the fresh detention order was invalid because it was not based on fresh facts that had arisen after the expiry of the previous detention, which is a mandatory requirement of Section 13(2) of the Act. The order was therefore in violation of the law, and the resulting detention was illegal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a fresh detention order under Section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act is valid if it is not based on fresh facts that have arisen after the date of expiry of the previous detention.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner challenged the validity of the fresh detention order dated August 28, 1969.
The grounds for the new detention order were identical to the grounds of the previous order from 1968.
A fresh detention order under Section 13(2) of the Act can only be justified by fresh facts that have arisen *after* the expiry of the previous detention period.
Since the new order was issued on August 28, 1969, a day before the previous detention was set to expire, it was impossible for it to be based on facts that arose after the expiry.
Therefore, the new detention order violates the provisions of Section 13(2) and is illegal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (State of Assam) did not present a substantive legal argument to defend the validity of the fresh detention order. Instead, they repeatedly requested more time from the court to obtain and present materials to justify the order.

cases.case_name: Hadibandhu Das v. District Magistrate, Cuttack and Another
cases.principle: A fresh detention order can be made on the revocation or expiry of a previous detention order only in cases where fresh facts have arisen after the date of revocation or expiry.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A fresh detention order, made upon the revocation or expiry of a previous detention order, is only valid if it is based on new facts that have arisen after the date of the previous order's revocation or expiry. Facts that arise during the period of the previous detention do not satisfy this requirement.
obiter: It is doubtful that a person in preventive custody could maintain links with associates outside of jail.
If a detainee was able to maintain such links, it reflects poorly on the persons in charge of their custody.
Detention of a person without trial, even for a single day, is a matter of great consequence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Under s. 13(2) what is required is that fresh facts should have arisen after the expiry of the previous detention. Facts arising during the period of detention are, therefore, not relevant when applying the provisions of s. 13(2). In the present case, the fresh order was passed on 28th August, 1969, a day b~fore the expiry, and it is obvious that no fresh facts could by that date arise and yet be held to have arisen after the date of expiry. The order dated 28th August, 1969 was, therefore, not at all justified under s. 13(2) of the Act and that order being in violation of the provisions of the Act has to be held to be invalid.
legal_tests_applied: A fresh detention order under s. 13(2) can be made on the revocation or expiry of a previous detention order only in cases where fresh facts have arisen after the date of revocation or expiry.
why_respondent_won: The main requirement of Section 13(2) is that a fresh detention order must be made on fresh facts which have arisen after the date of expiry of the previous order.
The fresh detention order was passed on August 28, 1969, a day before the expiry of the previous order, making it impossible for it to be based on facts that arose after the expiry.
Facts that arise during the period of detention are not relevant for the purpose of making a fresh order under Section 13(2).

The one additional ground provided—that the petitioner maintained links with associates while in custody—occurred during the period of preventive detention, not after its expiry, and therefore does not satisfy the requirements of Section 13(2).
